title: Information Technology Act, 2000 — Section 4 (Legal Recognition of Electronic Records)

content.overview: Section 4 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 gives legal recognition to electronic records. Where any law requires information to be in writing, typewritten or printed form, such requirement is deemed satisfied if the information is made available in an electronic form and accessible so as to be usable for a subsequent reference, subject to the Act.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Does a law require writing/print? (2) Is the information in electronic form and accessible for subsequent reference? (3) Any special form still required by the other law?
content.study:
s. 4 is a functional-equivalence rule. It does not abolish every special form requirement; check the other statute.

No new case invented.

sections.heading: Functional equivalence
sections.body: A legal requirement of writing, typewritten or printed form is deemed satisfied by information in electronic form that is accessible for subsequent reference.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.body: The electronic information must be accessible so as to be usable for a subsequent reference — mere existence is not enough if it cannot be retrieved/used.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.body: Other statutes may still impose specific form, attestation or registration requirements that are not displaced solely by s. 4.

sections.heading: Link to ss. 5–10A
sections.body: s. 5 recognises electronic signatures; later sections address secure records, attribution and contracts.

sections.heading: Method
sections.body: Identify the writing requirement; test electronic form + accessibility; check residual special-form rules.

examples.title: Statutory notice in email
examples.body: Where a statute requires a notice in writing, an accessible electronic notice may satisfy s. 4 unless the statute demands a specific non-electronic form.

hypotheticals.question: Does s. 4 make every paper form optional?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. It deems writing requirements satisfied by accessible electronic form, but other laws may still mandate specific modes.

distinctions.title: s. 4 electronic records vs s. 5 electronic signatures
distinctions.left: Legal recognition of information in electronic form for writing requirements.
distinctions.right: Legal recognition of authentication by electronic signature where signature is required.

misconceptions.trap: s. 4 abolishes all paper formalities in Indian law.
misconceptions.correction: s. 4 is a deeming provision for writing requirements; special statutory formalities may still apply.
